title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Tolle opens with the first flower as a metaphor for awakening: just as plants flowered after millions of years, humanity is poised for a leap in consciousness. He traces the perennial message of the great teachers — Buddha, Jesus — and diagnoses the normal human state as dysfunctional: identification with the mind. A 'new earth' means a transformed collective consciousness, and it begins with each reader.
p: Flowers, crystals and gems were humanity's first glimpse of beauty beyond utility
The teachings of Buddha and Jesus were early flowers of awakening in the human mind
Ego — identification with form and thought — is the root dysfunction of 'normal' life
The book's purpose is not to add beliefs but to trigger a shift of consciousness in the reader

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
chapter: Ego: The Current State of Humanity
s: This chapter defines the ego as the illusory self built from identification — with things, roles, opinions, nationality, religion. 'I' and 'mine' fuse mind with form, so losing possessions or positions feels like losing oneself. The ego lives on complaint, resentment, and being right, and even spiritual ideas become ego-property.
p: Identification with things: what you possess begins to possess you
Complaining and resentment are favorite ego strategies for strengthening itself
The ego's core illusion: 'I am right and they are wrong'
Truth needs no defense; wanting to be right signals identification with mind

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Tolle exposes the mechanics inside all ego: greed for more, superiority and inferiority, gossip, fault-finding, and the need to make others 'other'. Behind every ego pattern lies fear and a sense of lack. Recognition is liberation: when you see the ego in yourself impersonally, it is no longer the ego but an old pattern observed.
p: The ego's mantra is 'not enough' — hence endless wanting
Fault-finding and gossip strengthen the false self by diminishing others
All structures of ego are unstable; anger and violence arise from its fear
Seeing a pattern as 'the ego' rather than 'me' already loosens it

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
chapter: Role-Playing: The Many Faces of the Ego
s: The ego acts through roles: victim, villain, lover, parent, authority. Tolle surveys pre-established and temporary roles, the ego with a mission, and the 'sufferer' identity, showing how collective ego hardens into institutions. Letting go of self-definitions means meeting each moment without a role — simply as presence.
p: Villain, victim, lover: unconscious roles played to get ego needs met
Pre-established roles (parent, boss) become prisons when fully identified with
Happiness in role requires abandoning the role — true relating is person-to-presence
You are most yourself when you are not playing any role at all

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Tolle introduces the pain-body in depth: the accumulated emotional pain of the past that lives as a semi-autonomous energy field. It feeds on drama, negativity, and media violence, and it can be individual or collective — as in the pain-bodies of nations. Dense pain-bodies dominate whole lives until presence breaks their hold.
p: The pain-body is old emotion stored in the body, periodically demanding food
Unhappy thoughts trigger it; it then amplifies the unhappiness that feeds it
Entertainment and news often cater to the collective pain-body
Awareness of the pain-body as it arises is the beginning of freedom from it

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Freedom begins with recognizing the pain-body as it awakens — a flash of irritation, a dark mood, an urge to hurt — and staying present as the watcher. Presence severs the pain-body's link to thinking, so it can no longer renew itself. Tolle also addresses the collective pain-body of humanity and the role of presence in healing it.
p: Freedom from the pain-body starts with realizing that you have one
Catch it the moment it awakens; the alertness of presence transmutes it
The pain-body cannot survive your conscious presence — it needs unconsciousness
Collective pain-bodies (of nations, groups) are healed the same way: through awakened individuals

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
chapter: Finding Out Who You Really Are
s: 'Know thyself' is the chapter's axis: who you think you are is a story — memory, conditioning, roles — while who you really are is the aware stillness behind it. Abundance, Tolle says, is the felt fullness of life now, not future acquisition. Knowing yourself and knowing about yourself are different things entirely.
p: 'Who you think you are' is a mind-made story; you are the awareness beholding it
Gnothi Seauton — know yourself — means knowing the depth, not the story
Abundance is a state of being: fullness felt now, not things gathered later
Giving, acknowledging, and allowing reveal the self beyond the ego

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Awakening is the discovery of inner space: the dimension of stillness and awareness beneath the objects of consciousness. Tolle teaches noticing the space around things, the gaps between thoughts, and the aliveness of the inner body — shifting identity from the content of consciousness to consciousness itself.
p: You are not the content of consciousness but the space in which it appears
Inner and outer space mirror each other; awareness of one opens the other
Breath awareness and inner-body sensing are direct doors into inner space
The 'now' and inner space are one: presence is space-like awareness

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Tolle distinguishes inner purpose — awakening, being present — from outer purpose — what you do in the world. Inner purpose always comes first and concerns only this moment; outer purpose follows and changes over time. When the two align, what you do becomes a channel for consciousness, and the new earth begins through your life.
p: Inner purpose is to awaken; it concerns only your state of consciousness now
Outer purpose varies and is secondary; it is empowered only when aligned with presence
The journey has only one step: the one you are taking now
Success without presence still fails; presence turns any action into awakening

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: The closing chapter describes awakened doing through three modalities: acceptance, enjoyment, and enthusiasm. Whatever you do, do it in one of these states, or it is ego. Enthusiasm joins vision with joy and creates in harmony with the universe. The 'new heaven' — awakened consciousness — brings the new earth into being; 'the meek shall inherit the earth' means the ego-free human.
p: Awakened doing takes three forms: acceptance, enjoyment, enthusiasm
Accept what you must do, enjoy what you love, enthuse what aligns with your vision
Enthusiasm is creative energy aligned with the universe, never stress or struggle
The new earth arises as more humans live from presence — the meek inherit it

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: Biblical and literary references for each chapter — the scriptural sources of Tolle's quotations, from Revelation and Isaiah to the Sermon on the Mount, Luke, and Hafiz.
p: Chapter epigraphs and quotations traced to scripture and poetry
Sources include Revelation 21:1, Isaiah 65:17, Matthew and Luke, and Hafiz's The Gift

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
s: A short biography of Eckhart Tolle — contemporary spiritual teacher, author of The Power of Now and A New Earth, not aligned with any religion or tradition, whose teaching points to the transformation of consciousness as the next step in human evolution.
p: Tolle teaches a universal, non-denominational spirituality
His books have reached millions worldwide and been translated into many languages
His central message: presence is the next stage of humanity's evolution

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Defines clairvoyance as the power of seeing what is hidden from ordinary physical sight, explains its relation to the astral and mental planes, and distinguishes genuine faculty from common imitations.
p: Clairvoyance = clear-seeing beyond the physical senses
It operates through the astral and mental bodies
Genuine faculty differs from trance mediumship and imagination

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Describes full simple clairvoyance — seeing the astral or mental plane around one as clearly as the physical, including auras, thought-forms, and non-physical entities.
p: Full clairvoyance shows the subtle plane as plainly as the physical
Auras and thought-forms become directly visible
Requires full waking consciousness and self-control

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Covers partial clairvoyance — fragmentary or occasional glimpses of the subtler worlds — and why such flashes are unreliable without training.
p: Partial clairvoyance gives fragmentary glimpses
Untrained glimpses are easily misread
Discrimination and training make it dependable

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Explains intentional clairvoyance at a distance — deliberately directing the subtler senses to a remote place, its methods, and its limits.
p: The astral senses can be directed to a distant scene
Intentional remote viewing requires concentration and practice
Distance is no barrier, but accuracy varies with training

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Discusses semi-intentional space-clairvoyance, where the vision arises in response to a strong wish, anxiety, or emotional link rather than deliberate direction.
p: Vision arises from strong emotion or desire rather than will
Common in crises — seeing loved ones at a distance
The emotional link supplies the motive power

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Examines unintentional space-clairvoyance: spontaneous visions of distant events that come unsought, often in dreams or moments of passivity.
p: Spontaneous visions arrive without intention
Often occur in dream, illness, or relaxation
Their value lies in verification, not cultivation

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
chapter: Chapter 7. Clairvoyance In Time: The Past
s: Describes clairvoyance of the past: reading the akashic records — the indelible impressions of all events — and the degrees of accuracy possible.
p: The past survives as records on the higher planes (akashic)
Trained vision can read these records accurately
Reflections of the records at lower levels are distorted

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
chapter: Chapter 8. Clairvoyance In Time: The Future
s: Considers foreseeing the future: how far the future is determined, what can be seen of it, and the philosophical problem of free will and prevision.
p: The future is only partly predetermined
Prevision sees tendencies, not fixed events
Free will operates within the web of causation

title: Clairvoyance
author: C. W. Leadbeater
s: Outlines how clairvoyance may be developed: the dangers of hasty or selfish methods, and the safe, slow path of purification, concentration, and guidance by a competent teacher.
p: Forced methods (drugs, séances) are dangerous
The safe way is purification, concentration, and meditation
A qualified teacher is essential for real development

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: Sinnett’s preface to this last collection of his essays, gathering the fruits of forty years of theosophical study and reflection.
p: A late harvest of the author’s theosophical thought
Written in the maturity of the movement’s second generation

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: I. This World’s Place In The Universe
s: Sets our earth in its cosmic context — the planetary chain, the scheme of evolution, and the true scale of the world’s place in the universe.
p: The earth is one globe of a planetary chain
Evolution works through the whole scheme
Our world’s place is humbler and greater than men think

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On the future life — and lives: the conditions after death and the return to birth as parts of one continuous existence.
p: The one life runs on through death and rebirth
Devachan and reincarnation belong to one process
The future is as orderly as the past

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On religion under repair — how theosophy restores the decaying fabric of religion by recovering its esoteric meaning.
p: Exoteric religion is in decay
The esoteric key repairs the structure
Theosophy offers religion a new foundation

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: IV. Religion Under Repair: A Reply To Professor Lindsay
s: A reply to Professor Lindsay’s criticism — defending the theosophical reading of religion against an orthodox scholar.
p: A point-by-point reply to an academic critic
Defends the historical and philosophical basis of theosophy
Shows the critic’s reading of the sources to be superficial

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: V. The Occultism In Tennyson’s Poetry
s: Traces the occultism in Tennyson’s poetry — the poet as unconscious prophet of the ancient wisdom.
p: Tennyson’s verse is full of occult intuition
The poet’s vision outran his creed
Genius taps the same source as initiation

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: VI. Creeds More Or Less Credible
s: A survey of creeds — which parts of the world’s faiths remain credible when tested by the ancient wisdom.
p: Creeds are tested against the esoteric standard
What survives is the common core of truth
Dogma that fails the test must go

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: VII. Imprisoned In The Five Senses
s: On man’s imprisonment in the five senses — the limits of the materialist worldview and the windows that open beyond.
p: The five senses are a prison with narrow windows
Materialism is the philosophy of the prison
The inner senses open on a wider world

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: VIII. Our Visits To This World
s: On our repeated visits to this world — reincarnation restated as the plan of our education.
p: Life on earth is a series of visits
Each visit is planned by the soul’s own past
The school keeps us until we graduate

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: IX. The Masters And Their Methods Of Instruction
s: On the Masters and their methods of instruction — how the adepts teach, and how pupils are found and trained.
p: The Masters teach by their own methods, not ours
Pupils are drawn by their own fitness
Instruction adapts to the disciple’s need

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On the expansion of theosophical knowledge since the early days — how the teaching has grown and been confirmed.
p: The teaching has unfolded since 1875
Later research confirms the early outlines
Knowledge grows by the labour of students

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On the pyramids and Stonehenge — the monuments of the past as witnesses of the archaic science.
p: The great monuments encode real knowledge
Astronomy and initiation are built into them
They belong to ages orthodox history ignores

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: XII. Theosophical Teachings Liable To Be Misunderstood
s: On the theosophical teachings most liable to be misunderstood — and the corrections needed.
p: Some doctrines are easily distorted
Precision of thought is a theosophical duty
Misunderstanding spreads faster than truth

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: XIII. The Super-Physical Laws Of Nature
s: On the super-physical laws of nature — the extension of natural law beyond the physical plane.
p: Law does not stop at the edge of the physical
The subtler planes have their own physics
Science will one day annex them

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On the higher occultism — the spiritual discipline beyond the psychic, and its conditions.
p: The higher occultism is spiritual, not psychic
Its price is the surrender of the personal self
It is the narrow way of the saints and adepts

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
chapter: XV. The Objects Of The Theosophical Society
s: On the objects of the Theosophical Society — what they mean and how they should be worked for.
p: The three objects are examined in turn
Brotherhood is the first and greatest
The Society is an instrument, not an end

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On the borderland of science — psychical research and the phenomena where science and occultism meet.
p: The borderland is where proof is possible
Psychical research is science at the threshold
Its evidence points the occult way

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On archaeology and the relics of antiquity — what the monuments really testify about the past of man.
p: The relics point to forgotten civilizations
Orthodox chronology is too short
The monuments confirm the archaic teaching

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On cataclysms and earthquakes — the periodic destructions of lands and races in the light of the secret doctrine.
p: Cataclysms are part of the planetary order
Continents have sunk before and will again
The races migrate ahead of the doom

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: On poetry and theosophy — the kinship of the poet’s vision and the seer’s knowledge.
p: Poetry is the echo of the inner worlds
The poets are the uninitiated seers
Beauty is a road to truth

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: A closing note on the essays and their place in the author’s life-work.
p: The essays close the author’s long service to the cause

title: Collected Fruits of Occult Teaching
author: A. P. Sinnett
s: Notes and references for the essays.
p: Sources in the theosophical literature of the day

title: H. P. Blavatsky: The Light-Bringer
author: Geoffrey A. Barborka
s: Geoffrey A. Barborka’s 1970 Blavatsky Lecture — a portrait of H. P. Blavatsky as the light-bringer of the modern age: her mission, her name’s symbolic meaning, the founding of the Theosophical Society, and the light of the ancient wisdom she restored.
p: A lecture delivered at the Society’s 1970 convention
Blavatsky’s very name is read as symbolic of her mission
The lecture traces her life’s work: to bring the light of the archaic wisdom to the modern world
Her writings — Isis Unveiled and The Secret Doctrine — are presented as the treasury of that light

title: In the Outer Court
author: Annie Besant
s: Besant opens these addresses to students by explaining purification of body, emotions, and mind as the first requirement of the probationary path — the outer court of the temple.
p: Purification of the physical, astral, and mental bodies
Purity of motive matters more than outer observance
The outer court prepares the disciple for the inner temple

title: In the Outer Court
author: Annie Besant
s: Teaches the mastery of thought: the mind as an instrument to be trained through concentration, meditation, and the deliberate refusal of undesirable thoughts.
p: The mind is an instrument to be mastered, not suppressed
Concentration and meditation are the chief disciplines
Undesirable thoughts are starved by withdrawal of attention

title: In the Outer Court
author: Annie Besant
chapter: Lecture III. The Building of Character
s: Shows how character is deliberately built by thought and will, how habits are remade, and how the qualities needed for discipleship are gradually developed.
p: Character is built by sustained thought and deliberate will
Habits can be dissolved and rebuilt
Qualities required for the path are developed, not bestowed

title: In the Outer Court
author: Annie Besant
s: Uses the image of alchemy for the transmutation of the lower nature into the higher — turning the lead of passion and selfishness into the gold of wisdom and love.
p: Spiritual alchemy = transmutation of the lower into the higher
Passion transmuted becomes strength and devotion
The fire of aspiration drives the transformation

title: In the Outer Court
author: Annie Besant
s: Describes the threshold between the outer court and the inner life: the tests, the qualifications of discipleship, and the attitude of service that admits the aspirant to the Master.
p: The threshold tests sincerity, perseverance, and selflessness
Service is the passport to the inner life
The relationship to the Master begins in fidelity to duty

title: In the Outer Court
author: Annie Besant
s: Notes and references for the lectures.
p: References to theosophical and scriptural sources

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: “Ego sum qui sum” — the opening chapter sets the old axiom of Hermetic philosophy against modern pretension, introducing the existence of an ancient Gnosis and the theme that science has forgotten the soul of nature.
p: An ancient Gnosis underlies all knowledge
Modern science is challenged on its own ground
The Hermetic axiom frames the whole work

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: On the pride of modern science and its refusal to examine psychical phenomena; the rise of spiritualism and the phenomena that science could neither deny nor explain.
p: Science dismisses what it cannot explain
Spiritualistic phenomena force the question
Pride, not evidence, decides the orthodox verdict

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The mirror of the soul: clairvoyance, psychometry, and mesmerism — the soul’s own powers reflecting truths invisible to the senses.
p: The soul has senses of its own
Psychometry and mesmerism are cited as evidence
Earth and heaven cannot both reflect in an unpurified mirror

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: “I covet Truth” — a defence of free inquiry against both theological and scientific dogmatism, and a sketch of the astral light as the medium of occult phenomena.
p: Free inquiry is the condition of truth
The astral light is the great magical agent
Dogmatism, clerical or scientific, is the enemy

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The spirit of denial: a close examination of materialism, the theories of force and matter, and the unknowable behind both.
p: Materialism is criticized as self-refuting
Force and matter are aspects of one reality
The ultimate is unknowable to the senses

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: Hermes’ staff — mesmerism, the odic force, and the phenomena of healing and trance as evidences of the vital magnetic fluid.
p: Mesmerism demonstrates a real vital fluid
Trance and cure are natural, not miraculous
The ancients knew this force as the astral light

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: “Thou great First Cause, least understood” — the elements and the elemental beings; the unseen population of nature.
p: Nature is thronged with unseen intelligences
Elementals are the agents of many phenomena
The First Cause is beyond personification

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: Magic and its wonders: the feats of the thaumaturgists explained as natural powers, with accounts of the adepts of the East.
p: Magic is a science, not a superstition
Adeptship explains the marvels of legend
The feats rest on knowledge of hidden forces

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: On the borderland of madness: mediumship, obsession, and the dangers of the séance room; the difference between medium and adept.
p: The medium is passive; the adept is master
Obsession is the peril of uncontrolled mediumship
Purity and will are the safeguards

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The triad: the doctrine of the trinity traced through all ancient systems, and the septenary constitution that unfolds from it.
p: The trinity is a universal archaic doctrine
Every system veils the same triad
From the triad the septenary order unfolds

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: On the strange condition of the human mind that must exhaust error before daring to approach truth — psychological phenomena and the evidences of survival.
p: Error is the mind’s long apprenticeship
Psychological phenomena testify to the soul
Survival after death is argued from the evidence

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: Against the doctrine of uniformity: the so-called impossibilities of nature and the testimony to wonders through the ages.
p: Uniformitarianism is a dogma, not a proof
The records of wonders are worldwide
Nature’s possibilities exceed the textbooks

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: Alchemy: the dialogue of the alchemist and Mercury — the philosopher’s stone as both a chemical and a spiritual mystery.
p: Alchemy has a spiritual as well as a material sense
The transmutation of metals is defended as possible
The true stone is the regeneration of man

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The records of Sais: Egyptian wisdom, the Book of the Dead, and the immense antiquity of civilization claimed by the priests of Egypt.
p: Egyptian records run back thousands of years beyond chronology
The Book of the Dead is an initiatory work
Egypt is a key to the archaic science

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: India and her fakirs: the wonders of Hindu psychology, the phenomena of the yogis, and the living tradition of the archaic wisdom.
p: India preserves the oldest living occult tradition
The feats of the yogis are matters of observation
The wisdom of the Rishis underlies the work

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The Church as the would-be science of God: the contradictions of the sects and the failure of dogmatic theology.
p: Theology contradicts itself from sect to sect
Dogma has replaced inquiry
The chapter opens the indictment of Church Christianity

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: On hell and the doctrine of damnation — its origin, its absurdity, and its moral effect.
p: Eternal damnation is traced to its sources
The doctrine is shown to be unphilosophical
Its moral influence is condemned

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The story of Jesus: the gospels examined, their contradictions, and the question of the historical Christ.
p: The gospel narratives are compared and criticized
The historical problem of Jesus is raised
The Christos is older than Christianity

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The mysteries: the pagan initiations praised by Cicero, their teaching, and their suppression by the Church.
p: The mysteries civilized the ancient world
Their teaching was the ancient wisdom
The Church inherited and hid their forms

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The gnostics: “learn to know all, but keep thyself unknown” — the gnostic systems and their preservation of the esoteric doctrine.
p: Gnosticism is the link between pagan and Christian esotericism
Its systems are surveyed
The gnostic maxim defines the initiate’s way

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: On time and eternity, the Kabala, and the oriental doctrine — the curtains of yesterday and tomorrow.
p: The Kabala is introduced as a key
Eastern metaphysics underlies the discussion
Time is the veil of eternity

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The Druzes and the secret sects of the East — living survivals of the archaic doctrine.
p: Secret sects preserve the old teaching
The Druzes are examined as an example
Popular beliefs about them are corrected

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: On heresy, the Inquisition, and the crimes committed in the name of religion.
p: The persecuting record of the Church is exposed
Heresy-hunting is shown as policy, not piety
The victims were often the wisest

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The triad again: the Logos doctrine and the trinities of the religions compared.
p: All trinities are forms of the one doctrine
The Logos is the key to the gospels
Comparative religion confirms the unity

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: Satan: the origin of the devil-doctrine, the serpent of Eden, and the dualism of light and darkness.
p: The devil is a late theological invention
The serpent is a symbol of wisdom in the old books
Dualism is traced to its Persian source

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: Buddha and his teaching: the doctrine of the Awakened compared with Brahmanism and Christianity, and the meaning of nirvana.
p: Buddhism is presented as a religion of ethics
Nirvana is explained, not as annihilation
Comparisons with Christianity are drawn

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The concluding chapter: Tibet and the lamas, the living adepts, and the final synthesis — the identity of the ancient wisdom beneath all religions.
p: Tibet guards the living tradition
The adepts are real, living men
The book closes on the unity of the wisdom-religion

title: Isis Unveiled
author: H. P. Blavatsky
s: The author’s vast apparatus of notes and citations from ancient and modern authors.
p: Sources span the whole range of sacred and scientific literature
The notes are themselves an education in comparative religion

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: The compiler’s preface: how these letters of William Q. Judge — written to encourage a student — came to be gathered for the help of all.
p: The letters were written to one earnest student
They were published because they help all students
Judge wrote under the name of the recipient’s need, not his own fame

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: The signal is raised: do not think of the writer, but of the Eternal Truth — the opening letter sets the impersonal tone of all true occult guidance.
p: Fix the mind on the Truth, not the teacher
Personality worship is the first snare
The work is for all, not for one

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On entering the movement on the right basis — conviction of the truth itself, not enthusiasm for persons or phenomena.
p: Enter on the basis of conviction, not emotion
The movement needs steady workers, not admirers
The truth is its own credential

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On weariness in the work — the writer’s own tiredness confessed, and the remedy of holding on without expectation.
p: Even old workers grow weary
The gaping crowd is not the reward
Hold on without looking for results

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the method of inner work — reading, self-examination, and the gradual discovery of the way within.
p: Look within while reading the books
The way is found by doing, not by asking
Self-examination is the daily discipline

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On duty and inability: our duty is never to consider our ability, but to do the work that lies before us.
p: Duty is measured by the task, not the talent
Do the work; the strength comes in the doing
The feeling of inability is no excuse

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the inner bells — the hearing of inner sounds as a sign of progress, with a caution against making much of such signs.
p: Inner sounds are signs, not goals
Do not stop to admire the milestones
Progress is in character, not in phenomena

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the wish that adepts might be sent to help — the answer that the help is already nearer than we think.
p: The help is proportional to the effort
The Masters do not waste their messengers
The true helper is the awakened self within

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the periods of silence and waiting — when all oracles are dumb, the work goes on below the surface.
p: Silence is a season of the inner life
Waiting is part of the training
The seed grows in the dark

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On conversion: no one is converted to theosophy — each one who truly comes, recognizes it as something long known.
p: Theosophy is recognized, not adopted
The soul remembers its own
Do not argue men into the movement

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the three gunas of the Bhagavad-Gita — the qualities of nature and their play in the disciple’s life.
p: The three qualities bind the soul to action
Know them, and act without attachment
The Gita is the devotional manual of the path

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On illness and the balance of life — a word of counsel in serious sickness.
p: Illness has its karmic side
The inner attitude governs the outer issue
Courage is itself a medicine

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On chelaship — the questions of would-be disciples answered from the writer’s own experience.
p: Chelaship is not taken up by asking
The qualifications are shown in life, not in words
The Master finds the ready pupil

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On passing from the outer relation of teacher and pupil to the inner relation of the Lodge.
p: The inner bond succeeds the outer
The Lodge is a living unity
The relation is of service, not privilege

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: What may properly be said to earnest inquirers who prove their perseverance — the deeper teaching held for the persevering.
p: Perseverance is the test of fitness
The deeper teaching follows the proved student
Curiosity-seekers get the shell; the earnest get the kernel

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: The closing letter of the first series — a cooling draught for the athirst, and the parting counsel of the writer.
p: The letters end in benediction
The teaching is for the distressed and the striving
The work goes on after the letters cease

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: The second book of the letters — further counsel written in the later years.
p: The second series continues the same guidance

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: The foreword to the second book of the letters.
p: Introduces the later correspondence

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: A word from afar — the writer, distant in body, speaks of the old friendship and the unbroken inner tie.
p: Distance does not break the inner bond
The true friendship is of souls
The work unites those who serve it

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: A brotherly greeting in absence — the letter to be read impersonally, as from the movement to the worker.
p: Read the word impersonally
The message outlasts the messenger

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: A note held in trust — to be used later, when the word is given.
p: Some things are written for the future
Patience with sealed instruction is part of the discipline

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: A letter to the Theosophical Publication Society on the work of publication.
p: The publication work is part of the movement’s service
The printed word carries the teaching far

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On turning from legal quibbles to eternal matters — the relief of the eternal after the business of the day.
p: The worldly work and the eternal work must both be done
The eternal matters give rest to the mind
Do not let the day’s business eat the soul

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the devices of the enemy — attacks and misleading letters to be expected from unexpected quarters.
p: Opposition comes in disguise
The student is warned, not frightened
Discrimination is the shield

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On troubles shared — the writer’s sympathy and the likeness of the trials of friends.
p: The trials of students are strangely alike
Sympathy is a real help
The common struggle binds the workers

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On health and the row of the outer world — what matters and what does not.
p: The body’s health is a charge on the worker
The outer noise is not worth the soul’s peace
Keep the centre still

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the pressure of work and people — the writer’s crowded days and the cost of the public work.
p: The public worker pays in strength
Preparation and anxiety are part of the load
The work is worth the price

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On a message received — splendid and marvellously accurate — and the answer returned.
p: True messages carry their own evidence
Accuracy is the test of the inner word
The writer answers in kind

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On an erroneous idea in the student’s mind — the correction of a sentence that needed explaining.
p: Errors of idea breed errors of life
The correction is given plainly
The student is asked to think it through

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On news of one lying very low — the shock of the message and the refusal to believe it the end.
p: The writer will not believe the work is done
Fire of purpose outlasts the body’s weakness
Hope is an occult force

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On a letter of distress — the writer’s plain and comforting answer.
p: Distress may be written without shame
The answer is friendship itself
The dark hour is not the last hour

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the astral form of things — even clothes have their doubles on the other planes, for nothing in nature is without its subtle counterpart.
p: Everything has its astral counterpart
The subtle planes duplicate the physical
This explains many small mysteries

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the living whole — we are all bound together, and the thoughts and acts of one react upon all.
p: Humanity is one living whole
No thought is private in its effects
Responsibility is universal

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On the law and the strain of exertion — neither the general law nor the Lodge neutralizes the effects of overstrain on the disciple’s body.
p: The law does not repeal cause and effect for disciples
Overstrain has its price
Care of the instrument is a duty

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On theosophy without the name — the essential principles stated in many systems, for theosophy is the universal fundament.
p: The truth wears many names
Judge the teaching, not the label
The universal fundament is one

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On danger within — the real danger is not on the outside, though attempts come from there.
p: The inner danger is the greater
Outer attacks answer inner weakness
Watch the fortress of the self

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: To those he loves and who work with him — a letter of communion with the fellow-workers.
p: The bond of the workers is sacred
Love is the strength of the work

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On cold and hard feelings — a confession and a lesson in the misunderstandings of the workers.
p: Even the best workers misunderstand each other
Confession clears the air
The personal equation must be watched

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: On a night at the lodge — a vivid account of a meeting, the crowd, and the speaker.
p: The lodge meeting is the movement’s heartbeat
The writer reports the life of the work
Enthusiasm and order both have their place

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
chapter: Extracts On Theosophy And The T.S.
s: Extracts on theosophy and the Theosophical Society — Judge’s shorter notes on the work and its organization.
p: Short extracts on the Society’s life
The work and its workers are the theme

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: Tea-table talks — informal, homely conversations on the deepest things.
p: The profound in the dress of the familiar
Judge’s gift of simple speech on high themes

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: Gleanings from The Path — selections from Judge’s editorial work in his magazine.
p: The Path was Judge’s own journal
The gleanings are its ripe grain

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: From unpublished letters — further counsel not before printed.
p: The unpublished letters continue the same guidance
Personal counsel made general

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: From manuscript letters — notes gathered from the writer’s remaining papers.
p: Fragments from the writer’s papers
The same voice, the same counsel

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: The London and Paris letters — Judge’s correspondence from the European centres of the work.
p: Reports from the European field
The movement as seen from its old-world centres

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: Mr. Judge’s stories — the tales by which he taught, east and west.
p: Judge taught by stories as well as precepts
The tales carry the doctrine in parable

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: An occult novel — a piece of fiction used as a vehicle of the teaching.
p: Fiction as a vessel of the doctrine
The story form reaches where the treatise cannot

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: Biographical notes on William Q. Judge.
p: The outline of Judge’s life
His place in the founding of the Society

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge

p: Judge as co-founder with Blavatsky and Olcott
His American work and his Irish birth
The estimate of his friends

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
chapter: Last Days Of Wm. Q. Judge
s: On the last days of Judge — his passing and the close of his work.
p: The account of his final illness and death
The work he left behind

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: “My only friend” — a memorial tribute to Judge.
p: A personal memorial
The love the writer bore the teacher

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: Words of students and friends — testimonies to what Judge was to those who knew him.
p: The testimony of the fellow-workers
The portrait drawn by many hands

title: Letters That Have Helped Me
author: William Q. Judge
s: A sculptor’s appreciation — an artist’s word on Judge.
p: The artist’s view of the man
Form and character read together

p: Editorial notes on persons and events mentioned

p: Introduces the edition of the letters

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: A. Trevor Barker’s preface as compiler — how the letters were gathered, transcribed, and annotated, and the principles of the edition.
p: The letters were written to A. P. Sinnett between 1880 and 1884
Barker transcribed and annotated the originals
The compilers aim was fidelity to the documents

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: The preface to the second edition — corrections, additions, and the reception of the first.
p: The second edition revised and enlarged the first
New letters and notes were added

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: Barker’s introduction — the history of the correspondence, the circumstances of Sinnett and the Founders, and the story of the letters’ writing and transmission.
p: The letters passed between the Masters and A. P. Sinnett
Transmission was by occult means — precipitated writing
The correspondence shaped the early Society

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: The philosophical and theoretical letters — the core of the teaching: the eternal principle, rounds and races, karma, reincarnation, the after-death states, and the powers of the adepts.
p: The doctrinal heart of the correspondence
God, nature, and man explained esoterically
The famous letters on the septenary scheme are here

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: The letters on probation and chelaship — the conditions of discipleship, the tests of the candidate, and the relation between Master and chela.
p: Probation is the testing-time of the aspirant
The rules of chelaship are laid down plainly
Failures and their causes are candidly discussed

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: The letters concerning the “Phœnix” venture — the proposed journal and the plans for the work in London.
p: Concerns a publishing project of the London circle
Shows the Masters’ interest in practical details
The venture tested the loyalty of the workers

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
chapter: The London Lodge Of The T.S.
s: The letters concerning the London Lodge — its founding troubles and its place in the work.
p: The London Lodge was an early storm-centre
The letters guide its conduct and policy

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: The letters on spiritualism and phenomena — the true explanation of the séance room, the shells and elementals, and the misuse of occult forces.
p: Séance phenomena are explained astrally
Mediumship is contrasted with adeptship
Phenomena are the least part of the wisdom

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
s: The first appendix — supplementary documents and letters bearing on the correspondence.
p: Supporting documents for the main text
Includes related letters and memoranda

title: The Mahatma Letters to A. P. Sinnett
author: A. Trevor Barker (compiler)
